abstract: Obesity remodels the adipose secretome, yet the adipocyte-derived signals that preserve insulin sensitivity remain incompletely defined. Here we identify neuritin (NRN1), a GPI-anchored protein, as an obesity-suppressed adipokine that protects against insulin resistance. In white adipose tissue, Nrn1 expression increases after adipocyte-specific deletion of DNA methyltransferase 3A (DNMT3A), which occupies the Nrn1 promoter. In obese mice, higher adipose DNMT3A and Nrn1 promoter methylation accompany lower Nrn1 expression, reduced NRN1 release from white adipose tissue and lower circulating NRN1. In humans, adipocyte NRN1 expression and plasma NRN1 concentrations are inversely associated with body mass index. Increasing NRN1 expression in white adipose tissue or raising circulating NRN1 improves insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis in obese mice without altering adiposity, whereas adipocyte-specific Nrn1 deletion exacerbates diet-induced insulin resistance. NRN1 enhances adipose insulin signaling and glucose uptake, raises circulating adiponectin, and restrains inflammation, adipocyte hypertrophy, and lipolysis. Mechanistically, NRN1 engages FGFR1 on adipocytes, stimulating receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling. For cell-expressed NRN1, this association depends on native GPI-anchor processing. Pharmacological or genetic FGFR1 inhibition abrogates NRN1-induced insulin sensitization in vitro, and adipocyte-specific Fgfr1 deletion largely abolishes NRN1's adipose and systemic effects in vivo. This pathway converges on PPAR-gamma: PPAR-gamma antagonism blocks NRN1-enhanced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, whereas rosiglitazone restores this response in Nrn1-deficient adipocytes and largely corrects insulin resistance in knockout mice. Thus, NRN1 is a previously unrecognized adipokine that acts as a non-FGF signal through adipocyte FGFR1 and PPAR-gamma to preserve adipose function and systemic insulin sensitivity.
